standard.title: Print and screen text features
standard.description: understand how print and screen texts are organised using features such as page numbers, tables of content, headings and titles, navigation buttons, swipe screens, verbal commands, links and images
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can understand conventions of print and screen including how books and simple digital texts are organised at Foundation level. They have not yet systematically compared the full range of navigational and organisational features specific to print versus screen texts.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students understand how print and screen texts are organised using navigational and structural features including page numbers, tables of contents, headings, titles, navigation buttons, swipe screens, verbal commands, links and images.

nodes.label: Print texts use structural features
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify structural features of print texts — page numbers, headings, titles, table of contents — and explain what each one does.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two structural features in a print information text and explain the purpose of each.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and explain the purpose of page numbers, headings, titles and tables of contents in print information texts, and use these features to locate information.
wider: Compare structural features across different print text types — information book, magazine, dictionary — and discuss how features vary by purpose
Use a table of contents to locate specific information and evaluate its usefulness
success_criteria: Student identifies at least two print structural features by name
Student explains what purpose each identified feature serves for the reader

nodes.label: Screen texts use navigation features
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify navigation features of screen texts — navigation buttons, swipe screens, verbal commands, links — and explain how they are used to move through the text.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two navigation features of a screen text and explain how each is used.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and explain navigation buttons, swipe screens, verbal commands and links in screen texts, discussing how each allows the reader to move through or interact with the text.
wider: Explore how navigation features differ across different screen text types — informative website, e-book, educational app
Discuss how verbal commands and gesture-based navigation (swiping) represent different modes of interaction with a text

response_modes.reason: Students encounter many different screen interfaces but may not have a conceptual vocabulary for navigation features. Multiple screen text examples build the generalisation that navigation features serve the same orientation purpose across different interfaces.

success_criteria: Student identifies at least two screen navigation features and names them correctly
Student explains how to use a specific navigation feature to move through a screen text

nodes.label: Print and screen texts compared
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can compare how print and screen texts use different features to serve the same organisational purposes, and identify features unique to each.
nodes.minimum_width: Compare at least one print feature and its screen equivalent, explaining how they serve the same purpose differently.
nodes.typical_width: Compare the layout and features of a print information text with a screen text on the same or similar topic, identifying shared purposes (navigation, heading, image) served by different features.
wider: Discuss which features a reader might find easier to use in print versus screen for locating specific information
Explore how images serve structural roles differently in print (fixed position) versus screen texts (interactive, linked)

response_modes.reason: This node integrates understanding of print and screen features — students coordinate their knowledge of both to make a comparison, which is the descriptor's core demand ('comparing the layout of print and digital texts').

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Comparing print and screen versions of the same informational content is genuinely rich — it opens questions about how medium shapes reading experience and information access that advancing students can explore meaningfully.
success_criteria: Student identifies one feature that print texts have but screen texts do not (or vice versa)
Student explains how a print feature and a screen feature serve the same purpose in different ways
